The widths of the confidence intervals reflect the uncertainty inherent at each horizon. For the 1-day forecast, the narrow range (803 to 815) reflects the limited time for unexpected disruptions or variability; the system is unlikely to experience much change overnight. By the 1-week horizon, the confidence interval widens significantly (798 to 826), as there is more time for noise, unexpected events, or natural fluctuations to come into play. By the 1-month horizon, the interval becomes even wider (790 to 850), accounting for increasing uncertainty as more variables or long-term risks could influence the system in ways that are harder to predict.

The main risks or events that could push outcomes outside the stated intervals are unexpected shocks or volatile behavior in the system. For example, sudden external disruptions—such as economic shocks, news events, regulatory changes, or environmental factors—could cause outcomes to fall well outside the projected range. Similarly, if the system you're forecasting (e.g., a financial market, demand for a product, etc.) is fundamentally susceptible to abrupt shifts due to human behavior or other unpredictable forces, those could also result in outcomes beyond the stated intervals. In short, while the intervals attempt to account for typical levels of uncertainty, extreme or low-probability events could still cause surprises.
